decisions.adds: nothing

decisions.where: A response check, not a verdict about what it is, P2

decisions.cut: You don’t have to find out if it’s a guard immediately, and you may not be able to comfort it quickly. Just keep an eye on whether the way you’re responding to it helps you get clearer and steadier and less hooked.
decisions.already_said: [703] "Remember that you don’t have to know what it is. Find out if it helps to be warm towards it or to keep it at arm’s length, and keep your boundary either way."; [695] "so you end up safer, clearer, more loving, more grounded and less hooked."; heading [701] "A response check, not a verdict about what it is"
decisions.adds: Only 'you may not be able to comfort it quickly', a small reassurance. The rest is the two points of [703] (you don't have to know what it is; check whether your response helps), with the measure from [695].
decisions.loses: That one reassurance; [704] already ends the section with what to do if it doesn't help.
decisions.where: A response check, not a verdict about what it is, P4
decisions.why: the section's recap: the heading and the paragraphs before it say it

decisions.cut: (If you’re proud, you give it an opponent, and if you panic, you give it your nervous system.)
decisions.already_said: [708] "It becomes a center of attention if you fear it, and if you hate it, you give it a hook in you."; [707] "Your first instinct may be to fight it, banish it, hate it, show it that you’re more powerful than it is, argue with it, panic, turn completely into the frightened part of you, etc."
decisions.adds: Two more reaction-and-cost pairs (pride gives it an opponent, panic gives it your nervous system). They match 'show it that you’re more powerful' and 'panic' in [707], but the point (reacting out of fear feeds it) is already made by the first two.
decisions.loses: Two vivid pairings.
decisions.where: Do not fight from fear, P2
decisions.why: two more cases after the point is made (fear gives it attention, hate a hook)
